content:
Hi all,

I'm interested in the faithfulness problem for auto-formalization into Lean 4, i.e. checking that a Lean statement really captures the intended informal statement.

One commonly used check is to ask a second LLM to translate the Lean statement back into natural language, and then compare the result with the original informal statement.

I'm fairly confident this method has already been studied, and I'd like to know whether there are documented cases where it turned out to be unreliable. By "unreliable" I mean: the back-translated statement looked equivalent to the original, yet the Lean formalization was not actually equivalent to it.

Note that this requires a kind of double failure: the first model has to produce a wrong formalization, and the second model has to translate it back into something that looks equivalent to the original statement (so the errors somehow cancel or get hidden in the reverse direction).

What I found so far (none of it directly measures this failure rate):

  • Li et al. 2024, "Auto-formalize Mathematical Statements by Symbolic Equivalence and Semantic Consistency" (arXiv:2410.20936): uses embedding similarity between the original and the re-informalized statement, assuming that informalization is much easier and more accurate than formalization.
  • "Faithful Auto-formalization via Roundtrip Verification and Repair" (arXiv:2604.25031): reports that a non-trivial fraction of rules passing their roundtrip equivalence check still show semantic drift (measured via an NLI analysis).
  • "Beyond LLM Judge: Mechanical Verification for Agentic Auto-formalization" (arXiv:2610.20573): mentions a Lean statement that received a FAITHFUL verdict from semantic checks, including a back-translation check, because the checker missed a subtle mistake.

I haven't found a systematic study of how often a wrong formalization survives a blind back-translation, nor a catalogue of such cases. Are there known examples, empirical studies, or papers that quantify this? Any pointers would be appreciated.

Thanks!

Wow, nice citations. I wasn't aware the Michael Douglas or Clark Barrett had students working on this problem, it is good to see!

Regarding your question, I think it is quite hard to get a strong signal on how faithful any particular autoformalization pipeline is. Most Lean experts do not want to spend all their time reviewing AI slop just to collect a small amount of data about how accurate this or that framework is.

I think your best shot for benchmarking these systems is to find existing databases of correct/incorrect formalizations (ideally, datasets which are quite recent and thus may not be in your LLM's training data, although this can be quite tricky these days) and see if your system can identify these correctly.
